# Want to Lower the Cost of Living? Unrig our Democracy.


Going into the midterms, voters are feeling the squeeze in their wallets and need relief. The answer lies in holding accountable politicians who prioritize their wealthy benefactors over them.


[Deirdre Schifeling](https://www.aclu.org/bios/deirdre-schifeling) ,
she/her


,
ACLU


**Share This Page**


October 26, 2026


It’s no secret that Americans are facing an affordability crisis. In the weeks leading up to the midterms, voters are inundated with political ads recognizing that Americans are working harder, paying more and getting less. Housing, health care, groceries, utilities and other necessities continue to eat up family budgets and show no signs of stopping. For millions of people, the basic promise that hard work should make it possible to build a good life feels increasingly out of reach. Meanwhile, the richest 10% hold 67% of all the country’s wealth.


Voters are asking: If our elected leaders know how much Americans are struggling, why aren’t they doing more about it?


The answer is that our political system is designed to work for corporations and individuals getting richer at everyone else’s expense. And voters have noticed that the economy predominately works for those who have all the resources to sway politicians and elections. If we want to unrig the economy to address the people’s needs, we need to unrig our politics to allow ordinary people to take the driver’s seat.


The wealthiest pay lower tax rates than people who don’t have enough money for a full tank of gas. Meanwhile, politicians grow increasingly unaccountable to the people who elected them. Instead of solving problems for us, politicians entrench their own power, manipulate ballot access and sideline communities that don’t fit their vision of America.


Some executive branch officials and Congressmembers wield government power and taxpayer dollars to enrich their families and friends and punish opponents. They’re using prosecutions and investigations to silence individuals, organizations, and journalists. For playing ball, corporations get a nearly unfettered ability to price gouge, form monopolies, pollute our neighborhoods and abuse the trust and pocketbooks of American consumers with no meaningful oversight.


Voters across the political spectrum see through this game. They see a system rigged to insulate politicians from democratic accountability — to prevent voters from electing the government we want and holding its feet to the fire.

[New research the ACLU conducted](https://www.aclu.org/documents/global-strategy-group-gsg-memo-new-poll-results-voters-see-holding-corrupt-politicians-accountable-as-central-to-addressing-affordability) with the Global Strategy Group found that nearly half of voters across party lines agree: One of the biggest barriers to addressing the skyrocketing cost of living is out-of-touch, corrupt politicians who refuse to tackle costs for fear of alienating corporate benefactors. In fact, voters identified holding corrupt politicians accountable as the single policy that would do the most to improve affordability.


Moreover, a new Fox News poll revealed that[60%](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/fox-news-poll-cost-living-concerns-weigh-gop-midterms) of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption. A swing voter from Utah responded to our survey saying, “Special interest groups, wealthy people and businesses can spend millions to buy a spot at the table and a voice in decision-making, while we have people who can’t afford meals, housing or healthcare.”


And a Republican voter in Pennsylvania put it more plainly, “When the wealthy, lobbyists or corporations have greater access to influence politicians, it makes it more challenging to trust that the voice of the common person matters.”


If we want an economy that works for ordinary people, we need a government that works for all people. This cycle, voters have the opportunity to put the wheels in motion.


At the ACLU, our loyalty is to the Constitution, not to any political party or candidate. For more than a century, we have defended the principle that the government derives its authority from the people and must remain accountable to them. That principle is under extraordinary strain today.


We can endlessly debate about the best policies to lower costs, but that’s not the work of the ACLU. However, the foundation is the same: To tackle the affordability crisis, we need to tackle the accountability crisis.


For a start, end partisan gerrymandering and protect the freedom to vote so that politicians must answer to voters. Stop governments and companies from tracking our license plates, faces, and search histories so that they can manipulate and control us. Give us real accountability by letting people sue government agents and agencies who violate their rights.


What most Americans want is simple. They want the freedom to find a good job, afford a home, raise a family, make their own decisions and build a secure life. A functioning representative democracy does not guarantee any particular policy outcome, but it does guarantee that the people making decisions have to answer to the people living with the consequences.


The ACLU holds fast to the promise of a democracy that is truly of, by, and for the people. That promise is not abstract. It determines who the government listens to, whose interests it protects and whether average Americans have the power to demand change.


The economy we get is downstream of the government we have. If we want to unrig the economy, we have to unrig our democracy.

### ACLU Sues to Stop Unlawful Federal Intimidation of Naturalized Citizen Voters


CALIFORNIA — A coalition of civil rights groups today filed a federal lawsuit to stop an unlawful and discriminatory program by United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that systematically targets, investigates, and intimidates naturalized U.S. citizens. The lawsuit was filed on behalf of OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates, OCA-San Mateo, OCA-Sacramento, and Common Cause, represented by the ACLU Voting Rights Project, Asian Americans Advancing Justice – AAJC, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of Southern California, and Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California (AJSOCAL). Since August 2026, USCIS has run what it calls an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” aimed at tracking and investigating foreign-born citizens under the guise of voter eligibility checks. As part of this initiative, federal agents rely on outdated, error-prone data and questionable methods — including posing as individual voters to search private voter registration records on state election websites. As a result, thousands of fully naturalized American citizens are subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations, and potential disenfranchisement based on flawed government data. “The Trump administration is challenging voters and threatening states based off flawed and outdated data,” said Theresa J. Lee, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project. “These allegations are putting eligible voters — including naturalized U.S. citizens — at risk of disenfranchisement. The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like. We’re challenging both these unlawful actions and the unreliable data behind them, and we will fight to ensure that no eligible voter is targeted or silenced because of it.” The lawsuit aims to immediately stop the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) from continuing the Unlawful Voter Initiative. It also seeks to block the federal government from pressuring state election officials to withhold or discard valid ballots cast by individuals appearing on DHS’s unreliable lists. Additionally, the legal action demands a formal declaratory judgment establishing that the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act’s Uniform Standards Provision, the Privacy Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). “Our communities have spent generations fighting to overcome barriers to the ballot box, and we cannot allow government intimidation to become another obstacle,” said Thu Nguyen, executive director of OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates. “Instead of helping voters participate in our elections, federal agencies are using flawed information to investigate and intimidate the very people they are supposed to serve. These actions threaten to undermine years of progress in building trust and encouraging civic participation in immigrant communities. We cannot allow fear to keep people from exercising their right to vote.” “This administration knows its data is flawed and unreliable, but they’re using it anyway to scare eligible voters away from the polls. It’s a deliberate effort to spread unfounded lies and make people doubt our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomon, president and CEO of Common Cause. “When even one voter is targeted, all of us are at risk. Common Cause will keep fighting in the courtroom and in our communities to make sure every single eligible voter can cast their ballot without fear of government harassment.” “Naturalized citizens are U.S. citizens, with exactly the same right to vote as anyone born here,” said John C. Yang, president and executive director of Asian Americans Advancing Justice – AAJC. “The ‘Unlawful Voter Initiative’ was never designed to confirm citizenship, and election officials have found it erroneously flagging eligible voters. Purging or investigating voters based on their system errors punishes citizens for the government’s own mistakes. Asian American voters, many of whom are naturalized, are bearing the brunt of it. We are suing to send a message that no eligible voter should be subjected to this intimidation tactic. We urge voters to go to the polls. Do not stay home out of fear.” “Citizenship earned through naturalization is not second-class citizenship. Yet this administration is combing through immigration records to single out naturalized Americans, many of them Asian American and Pacific Islander, and to treat their right to vote as suspect. No other voters face this scrutiny. We are proud to stand with OCA and Common Cause to insist that every eligible voter, however they became a citizen, is treated equally under the law,” said Dahni Tsuboi, CEO of Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California. View a copy of the lawsuit here: https://assets.aclu.org/live/uploads/2026/10/001-OCA-v-DHS-Complaint.pdf


**Court Case:** OCA-Asian Pacific American Advocates v. Department of Homeland Security

### United States v. Alaska


Representing two Alaska voters, the League of Women Voters of Alaska, and Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union and ACLU of Alaska moved to intervene in United States v. Alaska, a frivolous lawsuit seeking to prevent from the State of Alaska from certifying its election results if the incumbent U.S. Senator does not win the election. The lawless suit asserts a single claim based on the purpose language of the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), that has no basis in any case, legal principle, or arguably tenable reading of the NVRA. We are seeking dismissal of this suit that aims to deprive Alaskans of their right to vote and right to representation.

### Federal Court Sides With Voters, Ruling DOJ Data Demands Violate Voter Privacy, States’ Election Authority


WASHINGTON, D.C. — A federal court sided with Common Cause and voters in their lawsuit against the Department of Justice (DOJ), ruling the DOJ’s campaign to consolidate sensitive voter data violates voter privacy and illegally intrudes on states’ authority over elections. The court’s decision protects eligible voters’ freedom to cast a ballot without fear that their personal information will be misused, shared without authorization, or weaponized to challenge their eligibility. “The Trump administration has repeatedly taken extreme measures to interfere with how elections are run, undermine confidence in the results, and create confusion,” said Ming Cheung, Senior Staff Attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project. “This effort to seize sensitive voter data is part of that same pattern, and today’s ruling makes clear that the administration cannot use the federal government to disrupt elections or put voters’ rights at risk.” Over the past year, the DOJ has demanded full, unredacted voter rolls from 49 states and Washington, D.C. These records vary by state but include sensitive personal data like home addresses, social security numbers, and voting history. The agency intended to compare state voter list data with the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) notoriously inaccurate Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system in an effort to identify suspected noncitizens on state voter rolls and demand that states revoke their voter registration. The SAVE system has repeatedly and mistakenly flagged lawful U.S. citizens as ineligible to vote. The ruling states that the court “vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more—a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans. When the federal government defies federal laws, our system of checks and balances permits individuals to turn to federal courts for recourse. And if they prevail, courts are duty-bound to step in under the Constitution.” This ruling comes after federal judges in 26 states plus the 6th Circuit dismissed the DOJ’s demands, ruling the agency’s attempts to consolidate voter data unlawful. With the 2026 midterms rapidly approaching, the DOJ’s actions are part of a coordinated attempt by the Trump administration to deceive the public with false election claims, disrupt how states run their elections, and deny results they don’t like. This ruling demonstrates how federal courts can serve as an important check on the Trump administration’s authority. “I never imagined I’d have to worry about whether my personal information was safe just for exercising my right to vote,” said Plaintiff Ruth Nasrullah from Texas. “Today’s ruling means that I can head into November’s election with more trust that my data – and my vote – are protected.” “After I found out I’d been removed from the voter rolls as an eligible voter, it felt like I had my right to vote wrongly taken away,” said Plaintiff Anthony Nel from Texas. “No other voter should have to go through what I did, and this ruling protects every eligible voter from having their registration mistakenly revoked for no reason.” “This is a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice. It’s time the Trump administration stop these desperate attempts to seize voters’ private data and take control of our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, Common Cause President and CEO. “Every voter deserves to know their private data is secure and that they won’t be wrongly denied their freedom to vote. We are proud to win this protection for those whose election officials failed them.” The plaintiffs are represented by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Protect Democracy, the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia (ACLU-D.C.), and the Democracy and Rule of Law Clinic at Harvard Law School. “The Constitution and federal law are clear: states are responsible for maintaining their voter rolls, not the federal government,” said Nikhel Sus, Chief Counsel at CREW. “We are grateful for this decision, which is yet another setback in the Trump administration’s larger illegal scheme to take over states’ constitutional roles and federalize election administration.” “If the federal government were genuinely concerned about election security, it would not even consider compiling sensitive voter records in a massive centralized database with so little regard for the risks,” said Jane Bentrott, counsel at Protect Democracy. “This database violates federal privacy laws and puts millions of eligible voters’ data in harm’s way. Today’s ruling is a win for voters, a win for national security, and a win for free and fair elections.” “This decision reaffirms a simple principle: safeguarding voters’ personal information isn’t optional.” said Laura Follansbee, staff attorney at ACLU-D.C. “We applaud this decision and remain committed to ensuring that every eligible voter can participate in our democracy without fear that their private information will be improperly collected or misused.” “It’s no surprise that the Trump administration’s misguided attempts to take over elections have failed once again,” said Larry Schwartztol, Professor of Practice and Faculty Director of the Democracy and Rule of Law Clinic at Harvard Law School. “Today’s ruling joins a growing list of courts that have rejected this administration’s efforts to seize control of voter data and election administration. The Trump administration does not have the authority to nationalize elections, seize voter data, or override the states’ role in election administration — no matter how many times it tries.”
